content.prompt: Part 1 — The neglected child
content.answer: Bholi, whose real name was Sulekha, was the youngest of Ramlal's seven children. When she was ten months old, she had fallen off the cot and damaged some part of her brain, and her speech became stammering and hesitant. Later, an attack of smallpox left her face permanently scarred with pockmarks. So the family treated her as an ugly, slow girl, and even her real name, Sulekha, was forgotten — everyone called her Bholi, the simpleton. Her parents neglected her, and her sisters, especially her elder sister, treated her with contempt. Bholi grew up feeling inferior and frightened, shunning the company of other children.

content.prompt: Part 2 — The village school
content.answer: When the village school opened, the tehsildar, during a visit, told Ramlal that he should send his daughters to school. Ramlal was reluctant to send his daughters, but for Bholi — plain and unmarried-able — he decided it would be a way of getting rid of her. So Bholi, for the first time, was dressed in clean clothes and sent to school. She was frightened of the teacher, but the teacher's gentle voice and kind smile made her feel safe. The teacher told her that her name was Sulekha, a beautiful name — and Bholi, hearing it, felt a new respect for herself. That first day, she learnt to say her name without stammering, and the teacher's love began to change her.

content.prompt: Part 3 — The marriage proposal
content.answer: Years passed, and Bholi grew into a young woman of about fifteen. Ramlal received a marriage proposal from Bishamber Nath, a rich businessman of the neighbouring village, who agreed to marry Bholi because he was attracted by her father's wealth and standing. Ramlal was overjoyed, and the family began preparations. But when the wedding day came, and Bishamber Nath saw Bholi's scarred face, he demanded a dowry of five thousand rupees — and then, even as the wedding ceremony was about to begin, he raised the demand: he would not marry her unless he received the money in cash before the ceremony.

content.prompt: Part 4 — The revolt and the new life
content.answer: Ramlal, desperate, agreed to give the money, and the marriage continued. But then Bholi spoke — for the first time in her life, clearly and without fear. She refused to marry Bishamber, calling him a "greedy beast" and telling him to keep his money. Everyone was stunned. Bholi declared that she would stay with her parents and look after them, and that she would teach the village children, and that no one could force her to marry against her will. The story ends with Bholi returning home — no longer a frightened, stammering child, but a confident, self-respecting young woman who had, in her own way, become the "cleverest" person in the family.

content.prompt: The power of education and self-belief
content.answer: The central theme is the transforming power of education and self-belief. Bholi, neglected and treated as a simpleton, is changed by her teacher's kindness and her years at school. Education gives her not only learning but self-respect: she learns her real name, learns to speak without fear, and finally finds the courage to refuse a greedy groom. The story shows that education, especially of girls, is the greatest weapon against oppression.

content.prompt: The position of women and the evil of dowry
content.answer: The story exposes the cruelty of dowry and the low status of women. Bholi is married off for money and her father's prestige; Bishamber demands cash even as the ceremony begins. Bholi's refusal is a revolt against this system. The theme is that a woman is not a commodity to be sold, and that the greed of dowry must be resisted by courage and education.

content.prompt: Overcoming prejudice and appearances
content.answer: Bholi is judged by her appearance — her pockmarked face and stammering speech — and treated as worthless by her own family. Her journey shows how cruel such judgments are: the "simpleton" proves the most intelligent and courageous person in the story. The theme is that true worth lies within, and that prejudice based on looks or speech is a blindness the educated heart must cure.

content.prompt: Bholi (Sulekha)
content.answer: Bholi is the heroine of the story. Born the youngest of seven children, she is scarred by smallpox and stammers from an early accident, and her family treats her as an ugly simpleton — even forgetting her real name, Sulekha. She grows up shy, frightened and full of self-pity. But two forces change her: the village school, where her teacher's kindness gives her self-respect, and the moment of crisis at her wedding, when she finds her voice and refuses the greedy Bishamber. Her refusal is an act of astonishing courage: she, who could hardly speak, declares that she will not marry a man who demands dowry, and that she will serve her parents and teach the village's children. She is the story's proof that education and self-belief can overcome even the deepest wounds of neglect.

content.prompt: Bholi's teacher
content.answer: Bholi's teacher is the quiet heroine behind her transformation. When the frightened, stammering child comes to school, the teacher's gentle voice and kind smile make her feel safe. She tells Bholi that her name, Sulekha, is beautiful, and she teaches her patiently, day after day. Her love gives the child something no one else had given her: respect. The teacher represents the power of the educated woman — the kind, patient guide who shows that the "dullest" child, treated with dignity, can blossom. Bholi's final ambition, to teach village children, is the teacher's gift returned to the world.

content.prompt: Bishamber Nath
content.answer: Bishamber Nath is a rich businessman of the neighbouring village, the groom chosen for Bholi. He agrees to the marriage only because of Ramlal's wealth and standing. He is vain, greedy and cruel: when he sees Bholi's scarred face, he insults her by refusing at first, and then agrees on the condition of a heavy dowry — five thousand rupees. Even as the wedding ceremony begins, he raises his demand, insisting on cash before he will proceed. His greed is his undoing: Bholi's refusal shames him publicly, and he slinks away. He represents the selfishness and greed that Bholi's courage must defeat.

content.prompt: Ramlal
content.answer: Ramlal is Bholi's father, a numberdar (village official) with seven children. He is a traditional man: he is reluctant to send his daughters to school, and he marries Bholi off for prestige and money. He treats Bholi with indifference, calling her "simpleton", yet he is not evil — he is a victim of the customs of his world, panicking when the marriage is in danger and willing to pay any dowry to save it. His surrender to Bishamber's demands shows the weakness of the old ways; it is his daughter who must teach him courage.

content.prompt: Girls must be educated
content.answer: The story is a powerful argument for girls' education. School gives Bholi self-respect, knowledge and the courage to refuse a greedy marriage. The lesson: education liberates — it turns a neglected child into a self-reliant woman, and it is the surest path to equality and dignity.

content.prompt: Courage to refuse what is wrong
content.answer: Bholi's refusal of the dowry-seeking groom is a lesson in moral courage. She, who once could not speak, finds the strength to say no to greed and humiliation. The story teaches that standing up for one's dignity — even alone, even against tradition — is a duty, and that self-respect is worth more than wealth.

content.prompt: How did Bholi's family treat her and why?
content.answer: Bholi was the most neglected child in Ramlal's family. Her stammering speech, caused by a fall as a baby, and the pockmarks left by smallpox made her seem ugly and slow to her parents and sisters. They judged her by her appearance and treated her with indifference and contempt: they forgot her real name and called her Bholi, the simpleton; her elder sisters made her do the household chores while they prepared for their own marriages; and no one thought of her education or future. Her parents even saw her as a burden — when the tehsildar advised sending girls to school, Ramlal agreed only because school would "get rid of" Bholi. The family's neglect filled Bholi with a deep sense of inferiority: she was afraid of people, avoided children and thought herself worthless. The story shows how cruel such neglect is, and how love and respect can heal what it wounds.

content.prompt: What role did the school and the teacher play in Bholi's transformation?
content.answer: School and the teacher transformed Bholi's life. On her first day, she was terrified of the classroom, but the teacher's gentle voice and kind smile made her feel safe — "the first time she had ever been called by anyone with affection". The teacher told her that her real name, Sulekha, was a beautiful name, and hearing it with respect gave the child her first taste of self-worth. Day after day, the teacher taught her with patience, and Bholi learnt to speak clearly, to read and write, and to believe in herself. Education gave her more than knowledge: it gave her identity (her name), voice (her speech) and dignity (her sense of worth). By the time of her marriage, the frightened stammering child had become a woman with the courage to refuse a greedy groom. The story's message is clear: education, given with love, can transform even the most neglected child — and that is why the educated woman is the hope of the village.

content.prompt: Value question: What made Bholi refuse the marriage at the last moment?
content.answer: Bholi refused the marriage because education had given her self-respect, and self-respect gave her courage. Bishamber Nath's behaviour revealed his true character: he demanded five thousand rupees as dowry, and then raised his demand even as the ceremony began, humiliating Bholi and her family. Bholi remembered her teacher's lessons — that she was a person of worth, not a commodity — and she saw that the man was greedy, not loving. Her refusal was a revolt against dowry, against humiliation and against the idea that a woman must be grateful for any marriage. She declared that she would stay with her parents, look after them and teach the village children, and that no one could force her. Her courage was the fruit of her schooling: the girl who could not speak grew into the woman who would not be bought. Her refusal teaches that dignity is not for sale.

content.prompt: How does the story criticise the dowry system?
content.answer: The story is a sharp criticism of the dowry system. Bishamber Nath, a rich man, agrees to marry Bholi only because of her father's wealth; on the wedding day, seeing her scarred face, he at first refuses, and then consents only on condition of a five-thousand-rupee dowry. Even as the ceremony is about to begin, he raises his demand, insisting on cash first — greed and humiliation exposed in full view of the guests. Ramlal, helpless before custom, is ready to pay anything. Bholi's refusal is the story's verdict: a woman is not a business deal, and a marriage based on money is not a marriage at all. By making the heroine of the story — the "simpleton" — the one who rejects the dowry-seeker, the author shows that the evil is not in the victim but in the system, and that courage, born of education, is the only real cure.

content.prompt: Describe the transformation of Bholi from a child to a young woman.
content.answer: Bholi's transformation is the heart of the story. As a child, she was the picture of neglect: scarred by smallpox, stammering from an accident, called "simpleton" even by her parents, she was shy, frightened and full of self-pity, shrinking from other children and the world. School began her change: her teacher's kindness gave her the first love she had known, her name Sulekha restored her identity, and her lessons gave her speech, confidence and dreams. As a young woman of fifteen, she was still plain and neglected, but within her grew a quiet strength. The wedding was her crucible: when Bishamber's greed insulted her, she — who once could not utter a sentence — spoke clearly and fearlessly, refused the marriage and declared her own plans for her life. The girl who was considered the family's greatest burden became its greatest pride, and the "simpleton" proved the cleverest of them all.
